chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) said: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Umar ibn Azineh, from Aban ibn Abi Ayyash, from Sulaym ibn Qays al-Hilali, from the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him): from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) that he said in his speech:

The scholars are two types: a scholar who acts upon his knowledge, he is successful; and a scholar who abandons his knowledge, he is destroyed. And indeed, the people of Hell will be bothered by the smell of the scholar who abandons his knowledge. And the most regretful and remorseful of the people of Hell is a man who invited a servant to God, and God accepted his call and he obeyed God, so God entered him into Paradise, but He entered the caller into Hell for abandoning his knowledge and following his whims.

Then the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: Indeed, the two things I fear most for you are following whims and long expectations. As for following whims, it diverts from the truth, and long expectations make one forget the Hereafter.

key_terms.آخِذٌ بِعِلْمِهِ: One who acts upon/holds onto his knowledge

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a successful scholar and a destroyed one according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Khisal emphasizes the critical link between knowledge and action, noting that the inactive scholar's presence even torments the inhabitants of Hell, underscoring the severity of neglecting one's own learning. Imam Ali (AS) contextualizes this by identifying 'following whims' (ittiba' al-hawa) and 'long expectations' (tul al-aml) as the dual roots of this spiritual failure, a theme central to Shia ethical theology. The narration serves as a warning that intellectual authority without practical application leads to greater accountability than ignorance.
